title: I'm Sorry But There's No Shortcut for This
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday argues that there is no shortcut to real knowledge or wisdom, and that the effort of reading and research is the point rather than an obstacle. He opens with Seneca's story of Calvisius Sabinus, a rich Roman who bought slaves to memorize Homer and the poets so he could appear learned, and reads it as a parable for outsourcing thinking to AI. Drawing on his own biography research and Robert Caro's dictum to 'turn every page,' he insists that assistants and tools can help locate material but cannot do the reading for him. He then credits Robert Greene, under whom he apprenticed, with teaching him to read rigorously: questioning sources, verifying context, and building a system for capturing what he reads. The essay closes with James Stockdale's line that the greatest educational fallacy is believing wisdom comes without stress, framing difficulty as the price and proof of genuine learning. The piece doubles as a launch note for his Read to Lead reading challenge, but the essay's argument stands on its own as a case for disciplined self-formation.
points: Seneca's Sabinus, who treated his slaves' memorized poetry as his own knowledge, becomes Holiday's parable for anyone who believes having AI access to information is the same as knowing it.
Holiday's distinction is that the goal is not to possess information but to become the person who did the work to get it, just as paying someone to lift weights will not make you strong.
His research practice follows Robert Caro's 'turn every page': assistants may track and scan sources, but the author must personally read every document.
Robert Greene trained him to go beyond 'the gist' by interrogating where a quote came from, whether the source is legitimate, and whether it holds up across other sources.
Great reading is framed as an active discipline of questioning, verifying, annotating, following footnotes, and organizing notes for later use.
quotes: People have always wanted to get something for nothing. They’ve always wanted to get the results without doing the work.

And he would insist, Seneca tells us, that summoning knowledge on demand from one’s staff was no different from summoning it from one’s mind. Indulging this notion that any readily available capability was effectively one of your own, a friend suggested Sabinus take up wrestling.

I know it isn’t, but I like to think of this as a parable about AI. It would be nice if someone could do your learning for you, if something could do your thinking for you…but that’s just not how it works.

Because as I’ve said before, the point isn’t to have the information, it is to be the person who has done the work to get the information. You can pay someone to lift something for you…but that won’t make you strong.
So my researcher can help me track stuff down, scan stuff, put it in little binders, but ultimately, I have to touch it all. Every damn page. I have to read it all.
To be a great reader, it’s not enough to read—you have to question, challenge, verify, and mark things up. You have to put books through the wringer and authors on trial.
The whole point of reading is that it’s hard, but that the hard is worth it. There is a payoff and that payoff is priceless wisdom.
Valuable things are usually hard-won. Wisdom, a sound and strong mind, is one of them.
